paragraphs.heading: What hemoglobin is
paragraphs.text: Hemoglobin is a protein containing iron that helps red blood cells move oxygen. It picks up oxygen in the lungs or gills and drops it off in the body's other tissues. There the oxygen feeds aerobic respiration, which powers the animal's metabolism. Nearly all vertebrates have it; the one exception is a family of fish called Channichthyidae.

paragraphs.heading: How much it carries
paragraphs.text: Leaving water aside, hemoglobin is about 96% of the weight of a mammal's red blood cell, and around 35% with the water in. Each gram can bind 1.34 mL of O₂. That lifts the blood's total oxygen capacity seventy-fold compared with oxygen simply dissolved in plasma. A single mammalian hemoglobin molecule can carry up to four oxygen molecules.

paragraphs.heading: How it is built
paragraphs.text: The name joins two words, heme and globin. Each unit of the molecule is a globular protein with a heme group tucked inside, and each heme holds one iron atom that can bind one oxygen molecule. The usual mammalian form has four of these units. The globin units are polypeptides, long folded chains of amino acids, and their order is read from genes. In human adults, the main form, hemoglobin A, comes from the genes HBA1 and HBA2 on chromosome 16 and HBB on chromosome 11.

paragraphs.heading: Other cargo
paragraphs.text: Hemoglobin carries other gases too. It takes away roughly 20–25% of the carbon dioxide the body makes, in a form called carbaminohemoglobin. It also holds nitric oxide, an important regulatory molecule, and lets it go at the same moment it releases oxygen. When there is too much glucose in the blood, some of it sticks to hemoglobin and raises the level of hemoglobin A1c.

paragraphs.heading: Beyond the blood
paragraphs.text: Hemoglobin and similar molecules also show up in many invertebrates, fungi and plants. In these living things they may carry oxygen, or move and manage other small molecules such as carbon dioxide, nitric oxide and hydrogen sulfide. One variant, leghemoglobin, pulls oxygen away from the nitrogen-fixing nodules of legumes so the oxygen does not poison them.

paragraphs.heading: When the genes go wrong
paragraphs.text: Hemoglobin sequences drift apart as species grow more distant. Humans, chimpanzees and bonobos share exactly the same chains, while humans and gorillas differ by one amino acid in each chain. Within one species, mutations create variants; many are harmless, but some cause inherited diseases called hemoglobinopathies. Sickle-cell disease is the best known, and it was the first human disease explained at the molecular level. A largely separate group, the thalassemias, comes from making too little hemoglobin, and all of these diseases lead to anemia.

paragraphs.heading: A molecule too big to believe
paragraphs.text: In 1825 Johann Friedrich Engelhart found that hemoglobin from several species had the same ratio of iron to protein. From the mass of iron he worked out hemoglobin's molecular mass, the first time anyone measured the mass of a protein. Colleagues mocked him, unable to accept that any molecule could be that large. Gilbert Smithson Adair proved him right in 1925, and in 1959 Max Perutz worked out hemoglobin's structure using X-ray crystallography, sharing the 1962 Nobel Prize in Chemistry with John Kendrew.
